result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.trophic_levels()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the trophic level of every node in a directed graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L36949-L37016){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.trophic_levels( weighted=None, attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Trophic levels](/assets/graphs/trophic-levels.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A food web drawn left to right by trophic level: grass G feeds rabbit R and mouse M, both feed fox F, and mouse and fox feed owl O. Grass is basal at level 1, the rabbit and mouse sit at 2, the fox at 3, and the owl, eating at levels 2 and 3, at 3.5, the top of the table." width="100%"} Trophic levels come from food-web ecology (Levine, 1980), where an edge points from prey to predator. Basal nodes, those with no incoming edges (plants), have level 1, and every other node sits one level above the average level of what feeds it, weighted by edge weight. The result is a continuous hierarchy: a node fed half by plants (level 1) and half by herbivores (level 2) gets level 2.5. The same idea measures position in any flow or dependency network: citation chains, supply chains, or the layering of a software system. Every node must be reachable from a basal node, or levels are undefined. Edge weights are used on a weighted graph (`Graph(weighted=True)`), unless `weighted=` says otherwise. Self-loops (cannibalism) count toward a node's diet. See also `trophic_differences()` and `trophic_incoherence_parameter()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to weight diets by edge weight. If `None` (default), follows the graph. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store levels in. If `None` (default), uses `"trophic_levels"`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns a dictionary instead of self. If `False` (default), stores the levels as a node attribute and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[dict[int, float], Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=` is `True`: a dictionary mapping node IDs to levels (basal nodes are `1.0`). If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is undirected, has no basal node, or has a node not reachable from one. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A small food web: the fox eats rabbits and mice (both level 2), so it sits at level 3; the owl eats mice (2) and foxes (3), so it sits at 1 + (2 + 3) / 2 = 3.5: ::: {#47abf312 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec web = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["grass", "rabbit", "mouse", "fox", "owl"]) .add_edges([("grass", "rabbit"), ("grass", "mouse"), ("rabbit", "fox"), ("mouse", "fox"), ("mouse", "owl"), ("fox", "owl")]) ) levels = web.trophic_levels(return_dict=True) {web.get_label_from_id(n): level for n, level in sorted(levels.items())} ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` {'grass': 1.0, 'rabbit': 2.0, 'mouse': 2.0, 'fox': 3.0, 'owl': 3.5} ``` ::: :::
